content: Vaginal bleeding refers to the loss of blood through the vagina in females. This can occur as a normal physiological response during the menstrual cycle in the absence of pregnancy or as a result of hormonal or structural abnormalities within the reproductive system. Vaginal bleeding can happen at any age, but it requires thorough investigation when it occurs in prepubescent girls or postmenopausal women. During pregnancy, vaginal bleeding may indicate a potential complication that necessitates immediate medical attention. The source of vaginal bleeding is most commonly the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. However, it can also originate from uterine or cervical lesions, the vaginal walls, or, in rare cases, the Fallopian tubes. In pregnancy, bleeding is often related to the pregnancy itself, though this is not always the case. Rarely, the bleeding may stem from the urinary tract (hematuria), although most women can distinguish between vaginal and urinary bleeding. Vaginal bleeding can also be a symptom of vaginal cancer. Causes of Vaginal Bleeding Life-Threatening Causes: Abdominal cancer Adenocarcinoma Bleeding disorders or clotting abnormalities Cervical cancer Choriocarcinoma Dysfunctional uterine bleeding Endometrial cancer or infection Fallopian tube cancer Fibroids (myoma, fibromyoma) Genital tract tumors Glassy cell carcinoma of the cervix Neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix Pelvic cancer Peritoneal cancer Primary malignant melanoma of the cervix Rectal bleeding Trophoblastic cancer Uterine cancer Vaginal cancer Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma Common Causes: Miscarriage or abortion Placental abruption Adenomyosis Amniocentesis Anovulation Antepartum hemorrhage Asherman syndrome Cervical ectropion, polyps, or infections Cervicitis Choriocarcinoma Contraceptive implants or intrauterine devices (IUDs) Decreased menstrual flow Dysfunctional uterine bleeding Ectopic pregnancy Endometrial cancer, hyperplasia, or infection Endometriosis Endometritis Endometrial atrophy Estrogen withdrawal Fibroids Foreign bodies in the vagina Genital tract tumors Hydatidiform mole Menopause or perimenopause Menstruation Ovarian cancer or cysts Pelvic inflammatory disease Placenta previa Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) Precocious puberty Pregnancy complications Uterine atony, polyps, or sarcoma Vaginal infections, injuries, or foreign bodies Vulvovaginitis Diagnostic Approach The diagnosis of vaginal bleeding often begins with a detailed history of the bleeding, a physical examination, and appropriate medical tests. A pregnancy test is typically performed, along with hormonal evaluations, a Pap smear, and a transvaginal ultrasound. If the bleeding is excessive or prolonged, a complete blood count (CBC) may be necessary to assess for anemia. Abnormalities in the endometrium may require further investigation through hysteroscopy with biopsy or dilation and curettage (D&C). Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for vaginal bleeding include, but are not limited to: Abortion or retained placental tissue Adnexitis Adrenal disorders Cervical cancer, polyps, or infections Ectopic pregnancy Endometrial polyps or hyperplasia Endometriosis or endometritis Hormonal imbalances or therapy Fibroids or uterine leiomyomas Hypothalamic or pituitary lesions Placenta previa or placental abruption Trauma or injuries Thyroid disorders Vaginal or vulvar cancer Vaginal infections or varices Treatment Treatment for vaginal bleeding is directed at addressing the underlying cause. Hormonal bleeding issues during the reproductive years, if bothersome, are often managed with combined oral contraceptive pills. Contraindicated Medications Vaginal bleeding is considered an absolute contraindication for the use of certain medications, such as hydroxyprogesterone caproate and dinoprostone. Complications Prolonged vaginal bleeding can lead to iron deficiency anemia, which may develop insidiously. Resolving the underlying cause of the bleeding typically corrects the anemia. However, some women may require iron supplementation or blood transfusions to improve their condition.
